children: 0844 ET - The August jobs report came in better than expected, and June and July were better than previously reported, too. June's report was revised up by 11,000 to 31,000. The change for July was revised up by 44,000 to 21,000, reversing a previously reported decline in jobs. Taken together, employment in the summer months was 55,000 higher than first reported. (jessica.coacci@wsj.com)

0843 ET - Markets increased their expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike on Sept. 16 after August U.S. jobs data came in stronger than expected. Markets price in a 61% probability of a hike, compared with equal odds of a hike or unchanged rates prior to the data, according to LSEG. Data showed 162,000 new jobs were created in August, triple the 53,000 forecast in The Wall Street Journal's poll of analysts. July job creation data were also revised upwards. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0833 ET - Hiring in Canada came off the boil last month, a possible pause after the recent recovery or a sign of heightened jitters as trade tensions between Ottawa and Washington rise. Employment declined in August by 41,700, much weaker than the 15,000 gain economists anticipated and after a cumulative increase of roughly 181,000 from April to July. Compared with last year, employment was up by 216,500. With the labor force contracting by 36,800 and the participation rate dipping to 65%, the country's unemployment rate held steady at 6.4% after a half percentage point drop over the prior three months. Adding to disinflationary signals, the rise in average hourly wages for permanent employees slowed to 2% from 3% in July. (robb.stewart@wsj.com; @RobbMStewart)

0829 ET - Yields on long-maturity U.K. government bonds, or gilts, risk climbing further as the U.K. could face more intense inflationary pressures than its eurozone peers, RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Mark Dowding says in a note. The U.K. lacks gas storage of its own, leaving it exposed to rising energy prices, he says. The Bank of England could raise interest rates in the coming months to tackle inflation which could cause long-dated gilt yields to accelerate, Dowding says. Thirty-year gilt yields surged to 5.904% this week, the highest since 1998, LSEG data show. (miriam.mukuru@wjs.com)

0756 ET - Sterling looks vulnerable over the coming months as the U.K. is expected to face increased inflationary and fiscal pressures, RBC BlueBay Asset Management's Mark Dowding says in a note. The U.K. is exposed to greater inflationary pressure from high energy prices than its eurozone peers as it lacks gas storage facilities, Dowding says. In addition, high government borrowing costs could put further strain on public finances and hurt the economy, he says. RBC BlueBay Asset Management has an underweight position on sterling as its sees few catalysts that would support a rally in the currency over the coming months. Sterling edges up 0.1% to last trade at $1.3533. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0752 ET - RBC BlueBay Asset Management is skeptical that Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi would favor too strong a yen, RBC BlueBay Asset Management's fixed income CIO Mark Dowding says in a note. "Ultimately, we are skeptical that Takaichi will want too much yen strength," he says. RBC BlueBay thinks that any forthcoming change in policy is more focussed on avoiding further weakness in the yen and domestic bonds, with this having the potential to further weaken Takaichi's own position within the ruling LDP, Dowding says. The dollar is last up 0.3% at 156.20 yen, having dropped to a one-month low of 155.27 yen overnight, LSEG data show.(emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0702 ET - The cost of euro credit default swaps is steady as market attention focuses on U.S. non-farm payrolls data due at 1230 GMT. The jobs data will indicate the state of the U.S. labor market and could provide clues on the future path of U.S. interest rates. Markets price in a 50% chance of a U.S. Federal Reserve interest-rate increase in September, LSEG data show. The iTraxx Europe Main index of euro investment-grade CDS is unchanged at 52 basis points, S&P Global Market Intelligence data show. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)

0652 ET - Thirty-year Japanese government bonds look worth buying with yields above 4%, RBC BlueBay Asset Management fixed-income CIO Mark Dowding says in a note. "We continue to highlight attractive structural value in 30-year JGBs above 4%," he says. He adds that there is "a sense that Japanese policymakers are taking the selloff in JGBs seriously, now that 10-year yields have breached 3%." Dowding also points to speculation that the Government Pension Investment Fund will substantially revise upwards its holdings of Japanese bonds within its asset allocation. The 30-year JGB yield hit a peak of 4.207% on Wednesday and last trades at 3.967%, according to LSEG. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0628 ET - The persistence of the energy-price shock and the eurozone economy's resilience mean the European Central Bank could be on course to raise its key rate in both September and December, BNP Paribas economists say in a note. The ECB is expected to raise rates next week and will likely also raise both its growth and inflation forecasts, supporting the case for further tightening, they say. Continued higher energy prices and a robust economy make second-round effects--of which there is so far limited evidence--more likely to materialize. Policymakers will still label risks to the inflation outlook as being skewed to the upside, the economists say. (edward.frankl@wsj.com)

0617 ET - China's trade growth is likely to pick up modestly in August, according to Goldman Sachs in a research note. On exports, high-frequency indicators such as shipping volumes point to a mild recovery, the bank says. South Korea's reported imports from China remained solid, GS adds. "On imports, the ongoing AI capital expenditure boom should continue to support tech-related nominal imports, consistent with strong Korean exports to China in August," GS says. The bank forecasts export growth to rise to 26.0% on year in August from 23.9% in July, and for import growth to accelerate to 32.6% on year from 27.5%. (tracy.qu@wsj.com)

0609 ET - The U.S. dollar rises while Treasury yields are steady ahead of August employment data at 1230 GMT. Yields retreated Thursday after Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller's comments pushed rate-hike expectations lower, to roughly equal odds of a rate increase and a rate hold at the Sept. 16 meeeting. Waller said he would support holding interest rates steady if next week's August inflation data backed it up. However, yields "remain at elevated levels" as an interest-rate hike is still expected before the end of the year, DHF Capital S.A's Bas Kooijman says in a note. The DXY dollar index rises 0.2% to 99.099, rebounding slightly from steep losses Thursday. The 10-year Treasury yield is steady at 4.762%, according to Tradeweb. (emese.bartha@wsj.com)

0559 ET - Yields on U.K. government bonds, or gilts, decline after the Bank of England's Decision Maker Panel data showed a slowdown in U.K. businesses' price expectations. The year-ahead own-price inflation expectation was 3.8% in the three months to August, down from 3.9% in the three months to July. The DMP data is likely to lead BOE monetary policy committee members to keep interest rates on hold in the near term while they wait for additional inflation data, Pantheon Macroeconomics economists say in a note. Ten-year gilt yields fall to last trade at 5.140%, from 5.171% prior to the data release. (miriam.mukuru@wsj.com)
